name: codevis
desc: Turns your code into one large image
why: Renders an entire codebase as one large image, turning source files into a strange visual map of structure.

brief.what_it_is: codevis is a command-line tool that takes every source code or UTF-8 encodable file in a folder and renders them all into one large image. It syntax-highlights files it recognizes. The output shows the shape and size of files rather than the exact characters, though a readable mode lets you zoom in and read the text.
brief.why_it_exists: The README does not state a motivation beyond the tool's output: images that show the shape and size of a codebase. It points to sister projects, codemov (video output) and codevis-gui, for related formats.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internals. It describes a single pass over a folder that renders each file into one image. Flags seen include --bg-pixel-color, --readable, --line-nums and --show-filenames, and --help lists more options.

brief.install_notes: Install the Rust programming language first, then run cargo install codevis. On Linux you may need to add cargo's binary folder (/home/username/.cargo/bin/) to your PATH if it is not already there. The Homebrew formula has no extra caveats. No accounts or special hardware are mentioned.
brief.standout: It turns a whole codebase into a single picture that shows structure and file sizes at a glance, rather than a file tree or a stats table. The readable mode lets the same image be zoomed into and read.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release dates, changelog, or commit information, and I did not check the repository's commit history or releases page.
brief.caveats: The image shows shape and size, not the exact characters, unless you use the readable mode and zoom in. Only UTF-8 encodable files are included. Installation requires building from source with Rust and cargo, which may take time. The README does not state a license.

entry.title: codevis
entry.tldr: Renders every source file in a folder into one large syntax-highlighted image, so you can see the shape and size of a codebase at a glance.
entry.deeper_look:
codevis walks a directory, picks up every source or UTF-8 encodable file, and draws them all into a single image. Files it recognizes are syntax-highlighted. The README puts it plainly: "These images show the shape and size of files, but not the exact characters inside the files."

The result is a kind of map. Big files look big, small files look small, and the colours hint at the language and structure. It is a different view from a file tree or a table of line counts, and it makes lopsided projects easy to spot.

There is also a readable mode. With --readable, the same image can be zoomed into until the text is legible, and --line-nums and --show-filenames add line numbers and labels. The README does not say why the author built it. It points to two sister projects, codemov for video output and codevis-gui, for related formats.

The underlying idea is treating source code as visual data rather than text. Once a codebase is a picture, you can compare projects, watch one grow, or just look at something you usually only read.
entry.install:
brew install codevis
# Homebrew builds and installs it with no extra caveats. Alternatively, install Rust and run: cargo install codevis

try_this.what_happens: Visualizes all files in the current directory and subdirectories, writing the image to ./output.png.
Does the same but saves the image under the name you choose.
Renders a readable version with a checkerboard background, line numbers and filenames, which you can zoom into to read the text.

entry.whats_unique: It turns a whole codebase into one zoomable picture instead of a file tree or stats table. The same image works as an overview and, in readable mode, as something you can read up close.
entry.caveats: The default image shows shape and size rather than exact characters, only UTF-8 encodable files are included, and the README gives no release or maintenance information.
